title: Jammy Boiled Eggs
subtitle: A set white and a fudgy, barely-gelled yolk, the ramen-shop egg
excerpt: Seven minutes in boiling water, then straight into an ice bath. The result is a white that peels cleanly and a yolk with the texture of thick fudge, neither runny nor chalky.
sourceNotes: The jammy boiled egg technique is associated with Japanese ramen cookery (ajitsuke tamago) but the timing has been widely adopted in modern British cooking for use in salads, grain bowls, and brunch plates.

recipe.batchNotes: Make up to 6 eggs at once. Store unpeeled in the fridge for up to 3 days.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keep unpeeled in the fridge for up to 3 days. Peel just before serving.

glossaryTerms.definition: A bowl of cold water with ice cubes used to rapidly stop the cooking of food by lowering its temperature quickly after it comes off the heat.
To maintain liquid at a temperature just below boiling, with small steady bubbles rising to the surface rather than a vigorous rolling boil.

content.text: The jammy boiled egg sits between a soft-boil and a hard-boil. The white is fully set and peels cleanly. The yolk has thickened to a dense, fudgy texture that holds its shape when you cut it rather than running. It's the egg that makes a salad feel substantial, that works in a grain bowl or on top of noodles, and that stores well enough to batch-cook on Sunday and eat through the week. The
ice bath
is not optional, it is what stops the cooking at exactly the right point and makes peeling dramatically easier.
What you need
You will also need a large handful of ice cubes for the ice bath.
Prepare the ice bath

Fill the large mixing bowl with cold water and a generous amount of ice. Set it next to the hob so you can transfer the eggs immediately when they come off the heat. This is worth doing before you start boiling, when the timer goes, you want to move fast.
Boil the eggs
Bring the saucepan of water to a rolling boil. Lower the
eggs
in carefully with the slotted spoon. Reduce to a steady
simmer
and cook for exactly 7 minutes. Set a timer, guessing is how you end up with the wrong result.
The ice bath stop

When the timer goes, transfer the eggs immediately to the ice bath with the slotted spoon. Leave them for at least 5 minutes, this halts the cooking completely and makes the shell contract slightly away from the white, which is what makes them peel easily. Do not skip this step and run them under a cold tap instead; cold running water is not cold enough to stop the carryover cooking inside a warm shell.
Peel and serve

To peel, tap the egg firmly on the counter all the way round, then roll it gently to crack the shell in a network of fine lines. Start peeling from the rounded end where the air pocket is, the shell tends to come away most cleanly from that end. Peel under a thin trickle of cold water if any fragments stick.

Cut in half lengthways to show the yolk. Season with sea salt flakes. Serve over noodles, tucked into a grain bowl, alongside a green salad, or simply on buttered toast with a pinch of chilli flakes. If storing, keep the eggs unpeeled in the fridge for up to 3 days and peel just before eating.
Troubleshooter

Yolk fully set and pale: the eggs cooked for too long, or were room temperature rather than fridge-cold (room-temp eggs cook faster). Stick to fridge-cold eggs and a strict 7 minutes. Make sure the water was at a rolling boil before you added them.

Shell tears the white when peeling: the ice bath wasn't long enough, or the eggs aren't quite fresh enough. Give them at least 5 minutes in the ice bath and add more ice if the water warms up. Slightly older eggs actually peel more cleanly than very fresh ones, the week-old egg in the fridge is ideal here.
Where this dish lives

The jammy boiled egg became a fixture of British food culture through the ramen boom of the 2010s. It appeared on restaurant menus in a marinated version (softened in soy sauce, mirin, and sake for a day) before crossing over into everyday home cooking. Its value is its versatility: it finishes a bowl of noodles, enriches a Niçoise, turns a grain bowl into a meal, and makes a quick lunch out of whatever is in the fridge. Making four at once and storing them means you always have a protein source ready to go.
